1:
The man is measured twice, by achievement and by retirement. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) holds that since Moses none so great had arisen, and recapitulates the work: his influence restored the Law of Moses to the affections of a people who had almost forgotten the lawgiver’s words and were becoming hardly distinguishable from the tribes around them; he taught the down-trodden Israelites who they really were, the chosen of God; and by creating a monarchy he welded the twelve divisions into one. His greatest work, Ellicott insists, was founding the prophetic schools, where men were trained to become in their turn the teachers of the people. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) dwells instead on the obscurity of his last years, which was not senility, since he still knew how to preside in a college of the prophets, but the consequence of Israel having rejected him, and of his own desire to be quiet. Let old people be willing to rest, Henry adds, though it look like burying themselves alive.

On when he died the chronologers reach opposite verdicts about what is knowable. John Gill (reformed) weighs the Jewish authorities, some making it four months before Saul and some seven, while Abarbinel thinks a year or two, which Gill calls most likely and indeed certain, since David was afterwards in Philistine country a full year and four months and Saul was not then dead; and the Jews fix the day as the twentieth of Ijar, for which a fast was kept. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) handles the same material and refuses the conclusion: Samuel lived about ninety-eight years and governed Israel before Saul for sixteen to twenty, and though the Jews say four months and Calmet two years, all this is very uncertain, and how long he died before Saul cannot be ascertained. Ellicott simply dates it about the time when Saul and David met at En-gedi.

Why the whole nation mourned is pressed by both voices, and they converge on one word. Henry says they had reason, for they had all a loss in him: the sons of the prophets had lost the founder of their college, and Samuel was a constant intercessor who prayed daily for Israel, so in losing him they parted with the best friend they had, and there was never more need of him than at that juncture. Those have hard hearts, he adds, who bury their faithful ministers with dry eyes. Ellicott fastens on the same emphasis through Stanley: we are told with peculiar force that all the Israelites, not one fragment only as might have been expected in a time of division, were gathered round him who had been the father of all alike.

Burial and flight raise questions of place. Henry notes he was buried not at Naioth among the prophets but in his own house, or the garden belonging to it, at Ramah where he was born. Clarke thinks it means not the dwelling-house but the tomb he had made for his sepulture, as the Syriac and Arabic seem to have understood it; Ellicott agrees it must be the court or garden, since burying him indoors would have occasioned perpetual ceremonial defilement. Of the wilderness they part company. Clarke places Paran on the confines of Judea or in Arabia Petraea between the mountains of Judah and Sinai, arguing from the history that it cannot have been far from Carmel. Ellicott reports that the Septuagint reads Maon instead, its translators doubting David’s camp lay so far from the scene of what follows, but holds the emendation unnecessary, since Paran seems to have given its name to the whole barren tract of which the wilderness of Judah would form part. Henry reads the move as fear rather than geography: having lost so good a friend, David thought his danger greater than ever and withdrew beyond the limits of Israel.
2:
Name and family carry a textual question. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) sets out the apparatus: the word means fool, from a root meaning to fade away, and was probably a nickname for his stubborn folly; and of his descent the Hebrew reads Kalibi, of the house of Caleb, while an alternative pointing gives according to his heart, and Josephus and the Septuagint with the Arabic and Syriac derive it from the word for dog and render him a cynical man. The Chaldee and Vulgate follow the received text, which Ellicott judges preferable. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reports the same Greek rendering, a doggish man, and derives the Latin nebulo, a knave, from this Hebrew root. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) takes the descent as the sting: Nabal inherited Caleb’s estate, Maon and Carmel lying near Hebron, but not his virtues, and a good extraction is a reproach to the man who degenerates from it.

On where he lived and what he was worth the notes turn moral. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) place Maon in the mountains of Judah and insist the Carmel here is not the promontory but the present Kurmul, scarcely half an hour north-west of Maon, the man being great through property with his establishment there. Ellicott agrees it is the small town and not the famous mountain. John Gill (reformed) reports Ben Gersom’s reading of Maon as a dwelling place, noted to show that Nabal lived not in a city but where his business lay. Of the wife, Ellicott calls her, with Stanley, the good angel of an ill-starred and boorish chieftain’s household, her name signifying whose father is joy and likely given by the villagers for her gladness-bringing presence. Henry turns the pairing into a maxim: riches are common blessings which God often gives to Nabals, to whom he gives neither wisdom nor grace; and many an Abigail is tied to a Nabal.

What David’s band was, and what its claim amounted to, is where the historical reading does most work. Ellicott observes that supporting so large a following must have been an anxious business, that contributions from the sheep-masters were not always willing, and that David’s position resembled a modern Arab sheik’s, his career as head of an army of free lances tending to popularise him among the southern tribes. Clarke presses the claim as a debt: David not only did the herdmen no hurt and took none of their flocks, but protected them from the rapacity of others, so that they were a wall unto us by night and day, where wandering hordes think they may exact provisions at will. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) adds a triple obligation: considering the licentiousness of soldiers and the necessities David was under, this was no small favour, which Nabal was bound in justice and gratitude and prudence to requite.

The greeting turns on an obscure Hebrew word, read three ways. Keil and Delitzsch admit it is obscure and was handled by the early translators merely by conjecture, the simplest explanation apparently being long life, a wish meaning good fortune to you. Gill takes it as a wish for the year to come: thus may it be for life, so that at the next shearing Nabal may be in as great prosperity as now. Henry accepts our translators’ addition, in prosperity, but turns it against the man, since those who live in pleasure are dead while they live, and calls it too high a compliment for such a muck-worm, for which David was well served by the rough answer. On the refusal they agree: Keil and Delitzsch say that to justify his covetousness he set David down as a vagrant run from his master, Clarke that it was unjust to refuse so reasonable a request, Gill that he answered in great wrath, as covetous persons do when they will not give.
12:
The messengers’ conduct is noticed before David’s. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) commends them for breaking off abruptly from such a churl yet governing themselves so well as not to render railing for railing, nor to take by force what ought of right to have been given; they told David, that he might do as he thought fit. John Gill (reformed) reads the restraint as judgement rather than meekness: they turned their backs without reply and treated him with silent contempt, but were determined to report the usage to David, who they doubted not would avenge the affront.

The muster is given exactly, the motive candidly. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) note that the churlish reply could not fail to excite his anger, so that he commanded his people to gird on the sword and started with four hundred men to take vengeance, two hundred remaining behind with the baggage. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reads the formality of the preparation and the size of the force as evidence of how terribly David was in earnest and how bent on wiping out the insult in blood. Henry supplies the words: David repented of the kindness he had done, saying that surely in vain had he kept all that this fellow had in the wilderness, since the man had requited him evil for good. Yet when we are so requited, Henry adds, we should not repent of the good we have done, for God is kind to the evil and unthankful.

What David resolved draws one verdict from three schools, and none softens it. Keil and Delitzsch judge that however intelligible his wrath may appear in the situation he was in, it was not right before God but a sudden burst of sinful passion, unseemly in a servant of God, and that by carrying out his intention he would have sinned against the Lord and against his people; the Lord preserved him from that sin, they add, by Abigail hearing of it just at the right time. Ellicott puts it in six words, that the anger is quite to be accounted for though not to be excused. Henry is the most unsparing. The resolution was bloody, to cut off all the males of Nabal’s house and spare neither man nor man-child, and the oath that ratified it was passionate; is this thy voice, O David, he asks, and can the man after God’s own heart speak thus unadvisedly with his lips? He who used to be dumb when reproached, and who had just spared the man who sought his life, will now spare nothing belonging to one who has merely affronted his messengers.

Why the affront found him unguarded is Henry’s explanation. From Saul, he observes, David expected injuries, and against those he was prepared and kept his temper; but from Nabal he expected kindness, so the affront was a surprise and found him off his guard. Ellicott weighs the speech of the young man who went to Abigail as evidence from someone in high authority on the farms, clear and decisive, and, coming in the heart of an episode most discreditable to David, bearing weighty witness to the admirable discipline and kind forethought of the son of Jesse: few men could have moulded a wild company of free lances into a force that was positively a blessing to the country rather than, as such bands usually are, a curse. Gill specifies the protection: a wall by night and day against the Philistines, the plundering Arabs of the wilderness, and the wild beasts. Ellicott takes Abigail to have often acted as peace-maker between her intemperate husband and his neighbours, and to have seen at once, with a clever woman’s wit, that grave consequences must follow; and of the servant’s name for his master he notes that Belial was no proper name but signifies simply worthlessness.
18:
Abigail acting at once, and without her husband, is defended two ways. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) praises the speed and the agency: it was no time to trifle when all was in danger, and being a woman of great prudence she knew better how to manage it than any servant, the virtuous woman looking well herself to the ways of her household. He holds she disposed of her husband’s goods without his knowledge not only lawfully but laudably, since it was not to gratify her own pride but for the necessary defence of a family otherwise inevitably ruined. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) argues it from necessity instead: the case was one of apparent necessity, and surely the necessity that dispenses with God’s positive commands might dispense with the husband’s right. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) note that she sent the gifts on before and followed behind, to appease his anger by meeting him in a friendly manner, without a word to Nabal of what she intended.

Whether the present was handsome or meagre is disputed. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) treats it as ample and the asking as modest: Eastern bread is thin and small, answering to our cakes; the bottles are goat-skins, the hide pulled off without ripping up and the leg-holes sewn, so the skin becomes one large bag; and out of three thousand sheep Nabal could not have missed five, the claim coming only at shearing, which was a small price for such services. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reports the opposite instinct among the versions: the Septuagint alters the measure to five ephahs, thinking the quantity ridiculously small for such a host, and Ewald would change five to five hundred. Ellicott holds the text, explaining that Abigail in haste provided a liberal present for David’s immediate followers, not the whole force. Keil and Delitzsch itemise it without comment, reckoning the roasted grain at an ephah and two-thirds.

The place of the meeting gets a careful gloss. Keil and Delitzsch read the hidden part of the mountain as probably a hollow between two peaks, which explains why the text says both parties came down: Abigail approaching from one side and David from the other, so that she lighted upon them. Ellicott adopts that explanation. John Gill (reformed) adds the tactic rather than the terrain: she sent the present ahead because the sight of it would in great measure pacify David and prepare him to hear her patiently.

David’s remembered words and his oath are read three ways and judged once. Ellicott treats the two verses as a parenthesis expressing what David felt and his justification in his own mind: Nabal had returned evil for good, since the band had long guarded his scattered flocks, and when a small favour was asked the churl threw in his teeth the taunt that he was a rebel and a runaway slave. Of the oath Ellicott calls the form an unusual variation, notes that the Syriac and Arabic read his servant David where our text has the enemies of David, and that the Septuagint cuts the knot by dropping the difficult word, but holds the Hebrew correct and the words as signifying David himself. Henry had already read it so, that David was going to say unto me and decently turned it off. Gill alone takes the phrase at face value, as a wish that God would give David’s enemies as much health and wealth as Nabal has, and much more. Clarke passes judgement without qualifying it: nothing can justify this part of David’s conduct, for whatever the provocation he had suffered no wrong, and his resolution to cut off a whole innocent family was abominable and cruel, not to say diabolic; and whoever attempts to vindicate it is, he adds, at least constructively a foe to God and truth.
23:
The speech is read as advocacy first. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) marks its method: by absolutely submitting to mercy without any pretence of justifying what was done, and rather aggravating it, she works upon David’s generosity, and there is hardly a head of argument the greatest orator might use here that she does not manage to the best advantage. Her opening he glosses as a formal substitution: let Nabal’s sin be imputed to her and punished in her, who offers herself as a sacrifice to David’s indignation. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reads the obeisance as evidence of what she believed about the man she knelt to, her tone betokening a consciousness that she addressed the anointed of Jehovah and future king; and she deprecates his wrath, representing her husband not merely as bad but as scarcely responsible.

Her central claim, that David was stopped rather than persuaded, turns on the oath. Ellicott follows the Speaker’s Commentary: since the oath affirms nothing it should be rendered, as true as that the Lord liveth, so true is it that the Lord hath withholden thee from blood-guiltiness. So confident is she of doing the Lord’s work, he adds, that before the armed band she speaks as though the danger were already past and David had real cause for thankfulness at being prevented from a wanton and wicked act. Of her prayer about his enemies, Ellicott takes her to dismiss Nabal as too insignificant to consider, so her wish is that the rest be equally harmless. Wesley presses it further: let them be forced to yield and implore thy pardon as Nabal now does by my mouth, and let the vengeance designed against this house fall rather on those whose inveterate malice deserves it more than a fool’s miscarriage.

That she speaks beyond her knowledge is agreed by both schools. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) say she gives such clear expression to her firm belief in the divine election of David as king that her words almost amount to prophecy; and they note that the evil not found in him means misfortune rather than wrong-doing, that thought arriving only later in the speech. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reads the clause as plain record: David had committed no act of this kind hitherto. Ellicott goes furthest: unconsciously she repeats words she may have heard in Samuel’s school by Ramah, thinking of the young captain before her as the future hero-king; but the unconscious prophetess never dreamed of that glorious and holy One in whose person, far down the stream of ages, the Eternal would make good her words.

On the bundle of life the exposition is one witness quoted twice, then enlarged. Keil and Delitzsch take the metaphor from the custom of binding valuable things in a bundle to prevent injury, and hold the words refer primarily not to eternal life in heaven but to the safe preservation of the righteous on earth in the grace and fellowship of the Lord; yet whoever is so hidden in that fellowship that no enemy can harm him, the Lord will not let perish, but will receive into eternal life though temporal death come. Ellicott quotes that paraphrase entire and builds on it, calling the verse one of the earliest definite expressions of belief in an eternal future in God’s presence, noting that it is now a favourite inscription on Jewish gravestones and that the Talmud has the souls of the righteous hidden beneath God’s throne; he even suggests it is the original of the apostle’s picture of the souls of them that were slain for the word of God. Clarke reads it without that apparatus: the life shall be precious in the Lord’s sight, supported by him who is the Spring and Fountain of life, while the enemies are cast off as a stone from a sling, which betokens both force and violence.
32:
The exchange is framed as a reproof well given and well received. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) sets the proverb over it, that a wise reprover upon an obedient ear is as an ear-ring of gold, and says never was such an admonition either better given or better taken, David acting on his own principle that if the righteous smite him it shall be a kindness. Most people think it enough to take a reproof patiently, Henry adds, but few will take it thankfully and commend the one who gives it; and Abigail did not rejoice more at having saved her husband and family from death than David did that she had saved him and his men from sin. John Gill (reformed) puts the same moment more plainly, that David heard her out and was overcome by her rhetoric and powerful arguments, and renders the word he blesses as her taste, her good sense, or, with the Targum, her discretion.

What David thanks, and in what order, is noticed by both the devotional and the grammatical reading. Henry observes that he thanks God first, for sending the check to a sinful way, since God is to be acknowledged in all the kindnesses our friends do us, and whoever meets us with counsel or caution or seasonable reproof we must see God sending them; and he thanks Abigail second, blessed be thy advice and blessed be thou. Of the danger Henry says David speaks as of something barely escaped: he was coming to shed blood, a sin he had a great horror of when in his right mind, and coming to avenge himself with his own hand, which would have been stepping into the throne of God, who has said that vengeance is his. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) summarise the reply in the same order and spend their note on one word, an imperfect carrying a perfect termination, which they take not for a copyist’s error but for an intensified form of the second person feminine.

That David broke a solemn oath rather than keep it is treated by two voices as the right thing, and the doctrine is the same. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) states it as a rule: it plainly appears that oaths whereby men bind themselves to any sin are null and void, and as it was a sin to make them, so it is adding sin to sin to perform them. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reaches the same conclusion by comparison. He notes that David, with his usual frank generosity, allows he was in the wrong in giving way to ungovernable passion and openly confesses that but for Abigail he would have carried out his purpose and stained his fair fame for ever; that his dark purpose had been to cut off root and branch the whole house of Nabal, the woman before him included; and that never had a more solemn vow been taken, yet before sunset he was convinced of its wickedness and deliberately broke it. Against that Ellicott sets two men who did not: Saul, who but for the people would have murdered his own son to fulfil the rash oath sworn at Michmash, and Jephthah, who ruthlessly carried out his wild and useless oath in the person of his daughter. Of the dismissal Wesley notes only that David showed his acceptance of her person by granting her request, and Gill that he took the present kindly for himself and his men, it being a gift fit for a prince.
36:
The feast completes the man, and finishes the portraits. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) counts him thrice dead here, beginning with dead drunk: he held a feast like a king’s though his guests were but his shearers, and it is very common for those most niggardly in any act of piety to be most profuse in gratifying a vain humour, a mite being grudged to God and his poor while gold is lavished to make a fair show in the flesh. He never thought he could bestow too little in charity, Henry adds, nor too much in luxury; and Abigail told him nothing, for being drunk he was as incapable of hearing reason as of speaking it, and to advise men in drink is to cast pearls before swine. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) draws the contrast with his wife as a contrast of eras: the husband churlish and unyielding, a friend of Saul and of the old disorderly state of things, falling at last a victim to his own untamed passions, is an extreme though not uncommon example of the leading Israelites before Samuel, while Abigail represents the nobler spirit after Samuel’s influence had worked upon the land.

What killed him is the chapter’s one medical question, answered four ways. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) makes it pure terror: he was thunderstruck, so terrified at what he had escaped that the fear overcame his mind, he became insensible to all around him, and died in ten days. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) gives the same cause a figure: he fainted through the horror of a mischief already past, as one who had galloped by night over a narrow plank laid on a broken bridge and, coming in the morning to review it, was struck dead with horror at the danger he had been in. Ellicott lays out two possibilities, fear, or a furious burst of anger that his wife should have humiliated herself before a man he hated, and judges fear the more probable. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) refuse the choice and make it compound: not his anger at the loss, nor merely his alarm at a danger he did not believe over, but also his vexation that his wife should have made him humble himself so, for he was a hard and self-willed man; and ten days later the Lord ended his life by a second stroke.

David’s reaction draws a criticism, and the narrative a caution. Wesley calls the blessing David pronounced over the news another instance of human infirmity. Of the proposal that follows, Wesley warns it was doubtless not made immediately upon Nabal’s death but some time after, such circumstances being commonly omitted in the sacred history, which gives only the heads and chief passages of things.

The marriages are law, property and politics. Clarke reasons that David had heard Saul married Michal to Phalti to cut off his pretensions to the throne, which justified him in taking Abigail or any other woman, it not being then unlawful to take several wives; and he supposes that by the marriage David probably came into all Nabal’s property in Carmel and Maon. Of the second wife he reports the view of many that Ahinoam was his before Abigail, being always named first in the lists and mother of his eldest son. Ellicott reads the giving of Michal as a deliberate breach: the act was high-handed and showed a fixed determination to break utterly and for ever with David, Phalti being presumably a chieftain Saul wished to attract to his fortunes; and her story does not end there, since after Saul’s death David would consent to friendship with Abner only if the princess were taken from Phalti and restored. Clarke adds that the man is called Phaltiel elsewhere, and his town probably lay in Benjamin, so Saul likely chose him for being of his own tribe.
